title: The Black Screen

post.author: u/starlite_night_jo
post.title: I work the night desk at an old motel. The key machine died, so I opened the closet nobody opens. Someone logs in there at 3:14 every night.

blocks.text: I run the night desk at the Starlite Motor Inn, sixteen rooms off the old highway. Since Friday the key-card machine at the desk makes dead cards. Guests check in at 2 AM, swipe, and get a red light. I've been walking people to their doors with the master key.

The new owner's nephew, Dale, says the card machine asks a computer in the back closet for every key. Nobody has opened that closet since Wren, the admin who ran the computers here, quit three years ago. Dale made me an account on it last week, my own username and password, and says he "tightened the security" on Friday.
The closet smells like warm dust. One beige box humming, one monitor, black, with a single blinking line: *starlite login:*. I typed my name and Dale's password, and it answered:

Dale texted that it's a terminal: you type commands instead of clicking, and the program reading them is the shell. The ~ means my home folder. Everything lives in the file system, folders inside folders, starting from one called /. I tried ls, which lists a folder, and cd, which moves you into one. In /srv/keys I found LAST_NOTE.txt, printed it with cat, and read the end three times:

blocks.title: LAST_NOTE.txt
items: Never rm -rf anything in /srv/keys. rm deletes, -r means everything inside too, -f means don't ask. No undo. No backup.
encode.sh has to stay executable, or the front desk can't make keys.
To change something you don't own, use sudo: do this as root, the boss of the machine. Be careful what you ask the boss for.
If someone logs in as me at 3:14, it isn't me.

blocks.text: Logs live in /var/log. I used grep, which prints only the lines containing a word, to search the login log for Wren:

Oct  4 03:14:07 starlite sshd[1907]: Accepted publickey for wren from 203.0.113.50 port 51190 ssh2
Oct  5 03:14:06 starlite sshd[1988]: Accepted publickey for wren from 203.0.113.50 port 49822 ssh2
Oct  6 03:14:07 starlite sshd[2073]: Accepted publickey for wren from 203.0.113.50 port 50417 ssh2
Every night at 3:14, three years after Wren left. The last one was this morning, while I stood at the front desk forty feet away.
Tonight at 3:14 I'll be sitting next to it.
Dale says just delete everything of Wren's. How do I get the keys working again, and what do I do about whoever logs in as Wren?

blocks.label: closet_tree.png

diagram.aria: The closet server's folders as Jo found them. At the top is /, the root. Under it are home, srv and var. home holds jo, where Jo starts, and wren, which answers Permission denied. srv holds keys, with LAST_NOTE.txt and encode.sh, the key script. var holds log, with auth.log, which shows the 3:14 logins, and keys.log, which is full of ERRORs.

blocks.caption: I drew the folders from what ls showed me. Wren's folder won't open for me. keys.log is all ERRORs since Friday.

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Wren's not using a password. *Accepted publickey* means a key login. SSH, the way to log in to a machine from far away, can check a password, or a key pair: a private key you keep and a public key you leave on the server, in a file called authorized_keys inside that account's home folder. Whoever holds Wren's private key gets in as Wren. Before anyone deletes anything, read the first line of that note again.

replies.author: u/starlite_night_jo
replies.text: Wren's folder just says *Permission denied*. Even ls won't look inside.

comments.author: u/dorm_rack_dev
comments.text: Permission denied is the machine doing its job. Every file has an owner and three sets of permissions: read, write and execute (run it as a program), for the owner, the owner's group, and everyone else. ls -l shows them, like -rw-r--r--. The command chmod changes them. Dale "tightened the security" on Friday and the cards died on Friday. Run ls -l on encode.sh.

comments.author: u/packet_ghost
comments.text: Two habits before any rm: pwd, which prints the folder you're in, then ls on exactly what you're about to delete. Practise in a sandbox, a folder of junk that's yours to wreck. And at 3:13 tonight, run tail -f /var/log/auth.log. tail shows the end of a file, and -f keeps watching it and prints each new line the moment it's written.

reply.prompt: Dale wants an answer before tonight's 3:14. What should Jo do about Wren's login? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Change Wren's password to something long and random. Then whoever it is can't log in as him.
options.part2: Dale changed Wren's password at midnight. At 3:13 I was sitting in the closet with tail -f running. At 03:14:07 a new line appeared: *Accepted publickey for wren from 203.0.113.50*. Same address as every night. Nobody had asked it for a password.
options.senior: A key login never uses the password, so changing it does nothing. To stop it, take the public key out of authorized_keys, then disable the account.

options.text: First copy /srv/keys somewhere safe. Then use sudo to remove Wren's public key from his authorized_keys and disable his account. Keep the logs as they are, and give everyone who needs the machine their own account and key.
options.part2: I made Dale copy /srv/keys to a USB stick first. Then, with sudo, we opened Wren's authorized_keys. One key, labelled *wren@backup-box*. We deleted that line and disabled his account. At 3:13 I sat in the closet with tail -f running. At 03:14:07: *Connection closed by authenticating user wren 203.0.113.50*. Then the same line every thirty seconds until 3:20. Then nothing. Somewhere out there, something still knocks every night. It just can't get in.
options.senior: Back up before you change anything. Remove the access, not the evidence. Give every person their own account and key, so you always know who did what. Then go and find where that private key lives.

options.text: Pull the closet server's network cable. Nobody can log in from outside a machine that isn't connected to anything.
options.part2: Dale pulled the cable at midnight. Nobody logged in at 3:14. Nobody got a room key either: the card machine at the desk talks to the closet over the same network. I walked guests to their doors with the master key until six.
options.senior: Cutting the network stops the login and everything else that needs the machine. It buys time to think, nothing more: Wren's key is still trusted the moment the cable goes back in.

options.text: Let Dale run sudo rm -rf /home/wren. No folder, no key, no ghost.
options.verdict: Burns the house to evict the ghost
options.part2: Dale typed it at midnight. The 3:14 login stopped. So did our only clue: Wren's folder held his notes about where the 3:14 visitor was sending the motel's guest file every night. Gone in under a second. No undo. No backup. Somewhere, a little computer still has three years of our guests' names, and we'll never know where.
options.senior: Deleting the home folder does remove the key, but it destroys the evidence and everything else that lived there, with no undo. Remove exactly the one line that grants access, and keep the rest.

sim.title: Sit down at the black screen
sim.lede: You're Jo at the closet's keyboard. This is a pretend Linux terminal with a small, pretend file system: nothing you type can touch a real machine. Type a command and press Enter, or type help to see them all. The up arrow brings back your last command. rm only works inside your sandbox folder, ~/sandbox.
sim.tryThis: Try the quest: find the last admin's note with ls, cd and cat. Use grep to pull the ERROR lines out of /var/log/keys.log. Look at encode.sh with ls -l, then fix it with chmod (you'll need sudo). Then run tail -f /var/log/auth.log and wait for 3:14.

explain.oneLine: No ghost. Dale's Friday change took the run permission off the key script, and a forgotten backup machine still holds Wren's private key, which the server never stopped trusting.

steps.title: The terminal is a conversation.
steps.text: The black screen is a terminal. You type a command and press Enter, the shell runs it, and prints the answer. pwd prints where you are. ls lists a folder, and ls -l adds each file's permissions, owner and size. cd moves you into a folder. cat prints a file, and less shows a long one a page at a time (q quits). grep prints only the lines that contain a word. tail prints a file's last lines, and tail -f keeps watching for new ones until you press Ctrl+C.

steps.title: Everything lives in one tree.
steps.text: The file system starts at /, the root, and branches into folders. /home holds each person's home folder, and ~ is short for yours. /srv holds data the machine serves, like the key files. /var/log holds the logs. A path such as /srv/keys/encode.sh is the route from the root to one file. A path that starts with / works from anywhere; one that doesn't starts from the folder you're in.

steps.title: Dale took away the x.
steps.text: ls -l shows -rw-r--r-- root root encode.sh. After the first character (a d would mean a folder) come three groups of three: the owner's rw-, the group's r--, and everyone else's r--. r is read, w is write, and x is execute, run as a program. There's no x anywhere. The auth log also records sudo commands, and it shows Dale's on Friday at 22:41: chmod 644 /srv/keys/encode.sh. In numbers, read is 4, write 2 and execute 1, so 644 means rw- for the owner and r-- for the rest. At 23:05 the card machine's next request got Permission denied, and every card since has been dead. The fix is one line: sudo chmod +x /srv/keys/encode.sh. Jo needs sudo because root owns the file, and sudo runs one command as root, the account allowed to do anything, after asking for your own password.

steps.title: The ghost has a key, not a password.
steps.text: Years ago Wren made a key pair with a tool called ssh-keygen and left the public half in /home/wren/.ssh/authorized_keys. At 3:14 a machine connects, says it's wren, and proves it holds the private half. The server checks the list, finds the key and lets it in. No password is ever asked, so changing it changes nothing. The label at the end of the key says wren@backup-box, and Wren's own notes, readable with sudo, say what that is: a little computer he set up to copy the motel's guest file to his place every night at 3:14. Nobody switched it off when he left. For three years it has been carrying guest data to a place nobody here knows.

steps.title: Why rm -rf is the most dangerous line on the machine.
steps.text: rm deletes. -r goes into every folder inside, and -f never asks and ignores errors. There's no trash can and no undo. GNU rm, the usual one on Linux, refuses by default to delete / itself, and that's its only guard: with sudo, /home/wren or /srv/keys would be gone in an instant. One stray space turns rm -rf old* into rm -rf old *, and the * then matches everything in the folder you're in. So: pwd, then ls exactly what you mean to delete, a backup you know works, and a second look before Enter.

diagram.aria: How the 3:14 login works. backup-box asks to log in as wren using key A. The closet server looks in /home/wren/.ssh/authorized_keys and finds public key A listed. It asks backup-box to prove it holds A's private key. backup-box answers with a signature made with private key A. The server writes Accepted publickey for wren. No password is ever asked for.

steps.label: ssh as wren, using key A · 03:14
prove you hold A's private key
signature made with private key A

steps.text: No password was ever asked for

explain.caption: Read top to bottom. The server never asks backup-box for a password. It only checks that the key is listed in authorized_keys and that the other side can sign with the matching private key. Taking the public key out of that list is what ends it.

fix.title: The fix: give back the x, take away the key
fix.text: Before changing anything, copy /srv/keys somewhere safe. Then run sudo chmod +x /srv/keys/encode.sh, and the card machine works again. For Wren: with sudo, delete the one line in /home/wren/.ssh/authorized_keys and disable his account, but keep his folder and every log, because they're the only record of what backup-box took. Then find backup-box and switch it off. From now on everyone gets their own account and their own key, admin work goes through sudo, and once everyone has a key, set PasswordAuthentication to no in the SSH server's settings, so there are no passwords left to guess.

limits: Removing one public key stops only that key. If Wren's private key was copied, or other old keys sit in other accounts' authorized_keys files, they still work. Check every account, and check again whenever someone leaves.
sudo is only as safe as the person typing. It can log what was run, but a log of sudo rm -rf in the wrong folder is a record of the disaster, not a way to undo it.
A backup you've never restored from is a hope. GitLab found out on the night it mattered that their backups weren't working.

head: Way in
Good
Bad
rows: Easy to start with. Nothing to install.
Can be guessed, reused or phished. Bots try them all day, so the auth log fills with failed tries.
The private key never leaves your machine and can't be guessed.
A lost or copied private key works until someone removes its public key from every server.
No open inbound port and no SSH keys to manage. Sessions can be logged.
Needs AWS's agent and permissions set up, and ties you to one provider.

explain.seniorTake: A server's terminal does exactly what you type, as whoever you are, with no undo. Look before you delete, give every person their own key, take keys away the day people leave, and keep a backup you've actually restored from. Most horror stories start with someone who was sure.

realWorld.title: GitLab.com, January 31, 2017
realWorld.text: GitLab's own post-mortem: while trying to get database replication working again, an engineer set out to wipe the PostgreSQL database directory on the secondary database server, thinking that's where they were, and ran it on the primary instead, a little before midnight UTC. They stopped it a second or two after noticing, but around 300 GB of data had already been removed. Then the backups let them down: one backup tool was an older version than the database and had been failing, and the emails meant to report the failures were being rejected. They restored from a copy about six hours old. GitLab.com was down for about 18 hours, and database changes made between 17:20 and 00:00 UTC that day were lost, including about 5,000 projects, 5,000 comments and 700 new user accounts. Git repositories and wikis weren't affected. One of their follow-ups: change the shell prompt on every host to tell hosts and environments apart more clearly.

realWorld.title: OpenSSH: how a key login works
realWorld.text: The OpenSSH manual describes it plainly. You make a key pair with ssh-keygen, which keeps the private key in your home folder and the public key next to it, with a .pub ending. On the server, ~/.ssh/authorized_keys lists the public keys allowed to log in to that account. When you connect, the client proves it has the private key, and the server checks that the matching public key is allowed. With a password, the password itself is sent to the server, encrypted, for checking.

realWorld.title: AWS: who holds the private key
realWorld.text: For an EC2 instance, AWS stores the public key on the instance, placing it in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on a Linux instance the first time it boots, and you keep the private key. AWS warns that anyone who has your private key can connect to the instances that use it, and that it doesn't keep a copy, so a lost private key can't be recovered. As an alternative to key pairs, it points to Session Manager, which gives you a shell on the instance through AWS.

asked: How do you give an engineer access to a production server, and take it away when they leave?
You need to delete an old folder on a production server. How do you do it safely?
interview.answer: Each person gets their own account and their own SSH key. Their public key goes in that account's authorized_keys, admin work goes through sudo so it's tied to a name, and password logins are turned off. When someone leaves, remove their keys and disable the account the same day, and look for keys copied to other accounts. Better still, use short-lived access such as AWS Session Manager, with no open SSH port or long-lived keys at all. For deleting: check which machine you're on and where you are (the prompt, hostname and pwd), ls exactly what the path or pattern matches, make sure there's a backup you've restored from, prefer moving the folder aside before deleting it, and have someone read a production command before you press Enter.

terms.def: Short for administrator: the person who sets up and looks after an organization's computers.
A username on a machine, with its own password or keys, its own home folder and its own permissions.
The device at a hotel desk that writes room keys onto plastic cards. At the Starlite it asks the closet server for every key.
A text window where you type commands to a computer and read its answers, instead of clicking.
The program inside a terminal that reads each command you type, runs it, and shows the result. On most Linux machines it's called bash.
One instruction typed into the shell, like ls -l /srv/keys: a program's name, then options and paths.
A setting added to a command, starting with a dash, like -l in ls -l or -f in tail -f.
The text the shell prints when it's ready, like jo@starlite:~$: who you are, which machine, and which folder.
How a machine organizes everything it stores: files inside folders inside folders, in one tree that starts at /.
A container for files and other folders. Also called a directory.
The folder at the top of the file system tree. Every other folder is inside it.
Each account's own folder, like /home/jo. Written ~ for short.
Short for your own home folder.
The route to a file through the folders, like /srv/keys/encode.sh. One that starts with / begins at the root; one that doesn't begins where you are.
Print working directory: shows the folder you're in.
Lists what's in a folder. ls -l adds permissions, owner, size and date. ls -a also shows hidden files, whose names start with a dot.
Change directory: moves you into a folder. cd .. goes up one level; cd on its own goes home.
Prints a whole file to the screen.
Shows a long file one page at a time. Space or Enter for more, b to go back, q to quit.
Prints only the lines of a file that contain a word or pattern, like grep ERROR /var/log/keys.log.
Prints the last lines of a file, 10 unless you ask for more.
Follow: keeps the file open and prints each new line the moment it's written, until you press Ctrl+C.
Holding Ctrl and pressing C. In a terminal it stops the command that's running.
Rules saying who may read, write or execute a file. The owner, the owner's group and everyone else each get their own three.
Read (see what's in it), write (change it) and execute (run it as a program). On a folder, x means you may go into it.
The account a file belongs to. Only the owner or root can change its permissions.
A named set of accounts that can share access to files.
A file with x permission, so it can be run as a program.
A small program written as a text file of commands, like encode.sh.
Change mode: the command that changes a file's permissions, like chmod +x encode.sh or chmod 755 encode.sh.
Permissions written as numbers: read is 4, write 2, execute 1, added up for owner, group and others. 644 is rw-r--r--; 755 is rwxr-xr-x.
The message you get when your account isn't allowed to do what you asked.
What chmod says when you try to change permissions on a file you don't own.
The account allowed to do anything on a Linux machine, also called the superuser.
Runs one command as root, if you're allowed to, after asking for your own password. It can log every command run that way.
Removes, or deletes, files. There's no trash can and no undo.
rm with -r (go into every folder inside and delete it all) and -f (never ask, ignore errors). The fastest way to lose a lot of data.
A safety rule in GNU rm, on by default: rm refuses to delete / itself. It protects nothing else.
A * in a path, which the shell turns into every name that matches. In rm old * (with a space) it means everything in the folder.
A safe place to try dangerous things, like a folder of junk that's yours to wreck.
A copy of data kept somewhere else, so you can restore it after a mistake. It only counts once you've restored from it.
Two matching keys for logging in: a private key you keep secret and a public key you can hand out. Only the private key can make a signature the public key accepts.
A file in an account's .ssh folder listing the public keys allowed to log in as that account, one per line.
A hidden folder in a home folder that holds SSH keys and settings.
The OpenSSH tool that makes a key pair.
The SSH server program. It listens for SSH logins and writes each one to the auth log.
/var/log/auth.log on many Linux machines: a log of logins and sudo commands, successful or not.
What sshd writes when someone logs in with a key: which account, and the address they came from.
The most widely used SSH software, made by the OpenBSD project. Its server program is sshd.
An OpenSSH server setting that says whether passwords are allowed. The default is yes; set it to no once everyone uses keys.
Stop an account from being used at all, without deleting its files.
A free software project. Most Linux machines use its versions of basic commands like rm, ls and chmod.
The main copy of a database, the one that takes all the changes.
A copy of a database kept up to date from the primary, ready to take over.
Copying every change from a primary database to a secondary, continuously.
A company whose website, GitLab.com, hosts code for millions of developers.
One project's code and its full history of changes, kept with Git, the most widely used tool for tracking versions of code.
A set of web pages anyone on a team can edit. On GitLab, each project can have one for its notes and documentation.
A write-up after an incident: what happened, why, and what will change. The good ones blame no one.
The key pair used to log in to an EC2 instance. AWS puts the public key on the instance, and you keep the private one.
An AWS Systems Manager tool that gives you a shell on a server through AWS, without an open SSH port or SSH keys.
A single, guarded server that people log in to first, before hopping to the servers behind it.
A port that accepts connections from outside the machine, like 22 for SSH.
AWS Identity and Access Management: the rules for who in your AWS account may do what.

atWork: If your team runs EC2 instances, open the EC2 console with read access and find an instance's key pair name. That's the public key AWS put in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys when the instance first started. Ask who holds the matching private key, and where. Then see whether your team could use Session Manager instead: AWS says it gives shell access without opening inbound ports, keeping bastion hosts or managing SSH keys, controlled by IAM and able to log every session. On any Linux machine you can already log in to, run ls -l ~/.ssh and cat ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, and ask of every line: does this key belong to someone who still works here?

recall.prompt: It's 11 PM. You're about to delete an old data folder on a production server with rm -rf. What do you check before you press Enter?

keyIdeas.idea: Where you are, and exactly what the path matches
Move it aside or get a second look instead of deleting blind

recall.model: Check which machine I'm on, from the hostname in the prompt, and whether it's the primary or a copy: GitLab's engineer was on the wrong one. Run pwd, then ls the exact path or pattern I'm about to delete, so I see everything it matches. Make sure there's a recent backup that I know restores. Then move the folder aside rather than deleting it outright, or have someone read the command first, and only delete it for good later.

recall.prompt: ls -l shows -rw-r--r-- root root encode.sh. Why can't the card machine run it?
options: Nobody has execute permission on it: there's no x
Only Jo is allowed to read it
recall.why: To run a file as a program, someone needs x. rw-r--r-- gives read and write to the owner and read to everyone else, with no x at all. sudo chmod +x encode.sh puts it back.

recall.prompt: Dale changes Wren's password. At 3:14 the login works anyway. Why?
options: It's a key login: the server checks the public key in authorized_keys and never asks for a password
recall.why: Accepted publickey means the visitor proved it holds the private key matching a public key in authorized_keys. The password is never involved, so the fix is removing that public key and disabling the account.

options: Runs chmod as root, which adds execute permission to encode.sh
Makes encode.sh readable only by root
recall.why: chmod +x adds x for owner, group and others. Root owns the file, so Jo's own account isn't allowed to change it; sudo runs that one command as root.

recall.prompt: Someone with access to your Linux servers leaves the company today. What do you do, and what do you not do?

keyIdeas.idea: Remove their public keys from authorized_keys
Look for keys copied to other accounts or shared logins
Keep their files and the logs instead of deleting them

recall.model: The same day: remove their public keys from every authorized_keys file they're in, disable their account, and check for their keys copied into shared or other accounts, plus any passwords they knew that others still use. Don't rm -rf their home folder: keep their files and the logs, because they may hold the only record of jobs they set up, like Wren's backup-box. Delete things later, on purpose, once you know what they are.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. The Starlite got a second server for its new booking site. Dale's plan: one shared account called admin, with one password that he, Jo and the new day manager all know, and SSH open to the whole internet with passwords allowed, "so nobody gets locked out."
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. What's wrong with Dale's plan, and what should they set up instead?

keyIdeas.idea: Everyone gets their own account, so you know who did what
Keys instead of passwords, with password logins turned off
Admin work through sudo, and access removed when people leave
Don't leave SSH open to everyone

coldCase.model: A shared password means nobody can tell who did what, you can't take access away from one person without changing it for everyone, and with password logins open to the whole internet, bots will be guessing it all day. Give each person their own account and SSH key, set PasswordAuthentication to no, and do admin work through sudo so every command has a name on it. Only let SSH in from places that need it, or use something like AWS Session Manager with no open port at all. When someone leaves, remove their key and disable their account that day.
